summary: A doubly linked list gives every node both a next and a previous pointer. That allows traversal in both directions and O(1) insertion or deletion at a node you already hold, at the price of one extra pointer per node.

sections.heading: Node structure
Insertion
sections.body: Update four pointers carefully, in an order that does not lose references.

sections.heading: Deletion in O(1)
sections.body: With a pointer to the node you can unlink it directly, no search for the predecessor needed (unlike a singly linked list).

sections.heading: Complexity
bullets: Insert/delete at head or tail (with a tail pointer): O(1).
Search and access by index: O(n).

sections.heading: Versus singly linked lists
bullets: Pros: backward traversal, O(1) delete of a known node, simpler tail operations.
Cons: more memory per node, more pointer updates (more bugs), poor cache locality like all linked lists.

sections.body: A circular list with a dummy head node means insert and delete never test for NULL at the ends: every real node always has a non-NULL prev and next. The Linux kernel's `struct list_head` is exactly this.
sections.code:
struct list_head { struct list_head *next, *prev; };
/* the list is circular; an empty list points to itself */

subtopics.title: Intrusive lists in the kernel
subtopics.summary: Embedding the links in your struct.

sections.body: Instead of nodes that hold data, put a `list_head` inside your own struct and recover the container with `container_of`. One node type serves every list and no extra allocation is needed.
Pair a hash map (key to node) with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. On access, unlink the node and move it to the front in O(1); evict from the tail when full. Both get and put run in O(1).

bullets: Forgetting to update prev of the old head or next of the old tail.
Freeing a node while another pointer still references it.
Breaking circular links in sentinel designs.

takeaways: Each node links both ways; delete a known node in O(1).
Costs an extra pointer per node and more pointer updates.
Sentinel nodes remove NULL edge cases.
Backs LRU caches, kernel lists, and undo history.
